issues.legal_issue: A difference between the courts where related suits were initially filed does not prevent a res judicata bar when both suits are tried by a court competent to decide them.
material_facts: The partition suit and the money suit were initially filed in different courts.
The money suit was transferred to the court hearing the partition suit, and that court tried and decided both suits.
The same issue concerning whether the brothers’ businesses were joint or separate was decided in both suits.
issues.conclusion: The initial difference in the courts’ jurisdiction did not prevent the decisions from supporting a res judicata bar because the court that actually tried both suits was competent to do so.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with Explanation II, determines a court’s competence irrespective of provisions governing a right of appeal. The relevant competence is that of the court which actually tried the suits. The Court followed Lortankutty v. Thomman and distinguished Narhari v. Shankar; it also noted that decisions made beyond a court’s jurisdiction cannot operate as res judicata.

predicates.appeal_challenges_one_of_related_suits: A party appeals from a decision in one of two related suits.
predicates.both_suits_were_decided_by_a_court_compe: The court that actually heard and decided both suits had authority to decide each of them.
predicates.same_issue_was_decided: The same issue was heard and decided in both suits.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns one of two related suits, the court that decided both was competent, and both decisions resolved the same issue, the initial difference in filing courts does not prevent res judicata.

issues.legal_issue: A difference in the right of appeal from two decisions does not prevent res judicata when the same issue has been finally decided and the earlier decision has not been challenged.
material_facts: The High Court heard and decided the appeals in the partition suit and the money suit together, issuing separate judgments and decrees.
The appellant could appeal to the Supreme Court as of right in the partition suit but had no equivalent right in the money suit.
The appellant did not challenge the High Court’s decision in the money suit, including by seeking special leave, and that decision became final.
The issue decided in the money suit was also material to the partition suit.
issues.conclusion: The different rights of appeal did not prevent the final decision in the money suit from operating as res judicata in the appeal concerning the partition suit.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the relevant question is whether the same issue was heard and finally decided, not whether each decision carried the same right of appeal. Explanation I addresses a decision in a former suit that has become final. The Court relied on Lortankutty v. Thomman and Bhugwanbutti Chowdhrani v. A.H. Forbes.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_a_decision_on_a_shared_issue and same_issue_was_finally_decided in another suit and other_suit_decision_was_left_unchallenged and appeal_rights_differed

predicates.appeal_challenges_a_decision_on_a_shared: A party appeals from a decision that concerns an issue also decided in another suit.
predicates.same_issue_was_finally_decided in anothe: The issue was heard and finally decided in the other suit.
predicates.other_suit_decision_was_left_unchallenge: The party did not pursue an available procedure to challenge the decision in the other suit, and it became final.
predicates.appeal_rights_differed: The party had a different right or route of appeal against the two decisions.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns an issue finally decided in another suit, that decision was left unchallenged, and the appeal rights differed, the difference in appeal rights does not prevent res judicata.

issues.legal_issue: A person litigating bona fide over a private right claimed in common may represent other persons with identical claims for purposes of res judicata.
material_facts: The partition suit involved several brothers claiming rights in family property.
The money suit was between two brothers, one of whom was also a party to the partition suit.
The money suit decided whether the brothers’ tobacco businesses were separate or part of a joint family business, an issue also relevant to the partition claims.
Applying the same decision to the common claim avoided the possibility of inconsistent decrees.
issues.conclusion: The other persons asserting the same common right could be deemed to claim under the person who litigated the issue, so the decision in the money suit could bind them for purposes of res judicata.
issues.legal_principle: Explanation VI to Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure deems persons interested in a private right claimed bona fide in common to claim under those who litigate about that right. The Court followed Kumaravelu Chettiar v. T.P. Ramaswamy Ayyar and applied the test of whether non-application of res judicata would produce inconsistent decrees.

predicates.proceeding_involves_a_shared_private_rig: The proceeding concerns a private right that is claimed in common by multiple persons.
predicates.a_person_litigated_bona_fide_over_that_r: A person genuinely litigated an issue concerning the shared private right.
predicates.other_claimants_have_identical_interests: Other persons have claims and interests in the right that are common or identical to those of the litigant.
predicates.same_issue_was_decided: The issue concerning the shared right was heard and decided in the litigation.

issues.definition: When a person bona fide litigates an issue about a private right claimed in common and other claimants have identical interests in that right, those claimants are treated as claiming under that person for the decided issue.

issues.legal_issue: An excessive delay in seeking permission to appeal from a final decision is not condoned when the application is made after the res judicata objection has long been raised and the decision discloses no error of law warranting further appeal.
material_facts: The respondents had raised the res judicata objection years before the appellant applied for condonation of delay to seek leave to appeal from the money-suit judgment.
The appellant’s application was made after a lengthy delay.
The High Court’s judgment in the money suit was based on the appellant’s admissions and disclosed no error of law warranting special leave.
issues.conclusion: The Court refused to condone the delay and dismissed the application for leave to appeal from the money-suit judgment.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that litigation should reach finality and held that the delay in seeking leave was too long to condone. It also considered that the challenged judgment disclosed no error of law warranting special leave.

predicates.proceeding_is_an_application_to_condone_: A party applies to excuse delay in seeking permission to appeal.
predicates.delay_is_excessive: The party waited an excessive length of time before seeking permission to appeal.
predicates.objection_to_finality_was_raised_earlier: The opposing party had raised an objection based on the decision’s finality before the delayed application was made.
predicates.challenged_decision_discloses_no_error_o: The challenged decision does not disclose an error of law that warrants permission to appeal.

issues.definition: In an application to excuse delay in seeking permission to appeal, an excessive delay, an earlier objection based on finality, and no apparent legal error warranting permission result in the delay not being condoned.
